title: Israel Struck Beirut Hours After the Truce Was Announced. The Iran Deal India Needs Just Got Harder.
excerpt: A hundred days into the conflict, every Israeli escalation in Lebanon pushes the Hormuz reopening further away — and India's oil lifeline with it.
body:
On Sunday, Israel struck the southern outskirts of Beirut for the first time since the United States announced a truce plan for Lebanon last week. An influential Iranian lawmaker responded on X with a threat: "Look at the sky of the occupied territories tonight."

The strike, ordered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in response to two Hezbollah projectiles intercepted over the border, did not just fracture a fragile ceasefire. It complicated the broader diplomatic architecture that India has been quietly counting on — an Iran deal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and relieve the worst energy supply crisis in modern history.

One hundred days into the conflict, the calculus for New Delhi remains stubbornly simple: no Iran deal means no Hormuz, and no Hormuz means India keeps paying a war premium for every barrel of oil it imports.

## The Lebanon Knot

Iran has repeatedly stated that any peace agreement with the United States depends on a ceasefire holding in Lebanon. The logic is straightforward: Tehran views Hezbollah as a strategic asset and Lebanon as a front it cannot afford to concede while negotiating with Washington.

Trump reportedly rebuked Netanyahu with obscenities during a phone call last week, pressuring Israel to scale back its campaign. Netanyahu agreed to the latest truce plan with the Lebanese government. But Israel has never fully halted its operations in Lebanon, and Hezbollah — which was not party to the truce and faces dismantlement under its terms — has continued attacking.

Sunday's strike on Dahiyeh, the Hezbollah stronghold in southern Beirut, signals that Israel's operational posture has not meaningfully changed. For Iran, that is grounds to delay substantive negotiations indefinitely. The Institute for the Study of War reported on Saturday that Tehran has suspended talks until a complete ceasefire in Lebanon is achieved — using Lebanon as leverage to avoid concessions on its nuclear programme and the strait.

## What the Oil Market Has Priced In

The energy market's response to 100 days of war has been the conflict's most counterintuitive development. When the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial shipping on February 28, Brent crude surged past $120 a barrel. Analysts warned of $150 to $200 oil.

Instead, Brent has stabilised around $100 — and West Texas Intermediate crossed that mark on Sunday evening. The premium for immediate physical deliveries, which hit $36 per barrel in early April, has fallen to roughly $2, according to JPMorgan research.

The reason is adaptation, not resolution. Saudi Arabia and the UAE increased pipeline shipments that bypass the strait. U.S. crude exports hit records. Governments released hundreds of millions of barrels from emergency reserves — the IEA's 400-million-barrel release on March 11 was its largest ever. And demand destruction did the rest: Goldman Sachs estimates the war cut global oil consumption by four to five million barrels per day in April alone. China's crude imports fell by roughly four million barrels a day from a year ago.

But as Barron's cautioned this week, the energy market is far from out of the woods. Emergency reserves cover only about 20 days of normal Hormuz flows. OPEC+ agreed on Sunday to a fourth consecutive monthly output hike — but the group's actual production has collapsed, averaging 33.19 million barrels per day in April versus 42.77 million in February, because Gulf members simply cannot ship.

## India's Adaptation Has Limits

India has responded to the crisis with aggressive diversification. Imports from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria have risen sharply. Venezuela is now India's fourth-largest oil supplier, with shipments hitting 427,000 barrels per day in May — nearly double April's figure. Russian oil continues to flow at around 1.9 million barrels per day.

But replacing 10 million barrels of daily Hormuz supply through alternative routes is not a permanent solution. Freight costs have risen. Insurance premiums on Gulf routes have spiked. The rupee is under sustained pressure from the elevated import bill. And U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright acknowledged on Sunday that the strait is not safe for commercial ships — a reality he said would persist until the war ends.

"We're going to see some elevated pricing," Wright told NBC's Meet the Press.

## The Diplomatic Bottleneck

The path to a deal runs through three interdependent negotiations: a U.S.-Iran interim agreement to halt the war, a Lebanese ceasefire that satisfies Tehran, and an OPEC+ framework that can actually deliver the barrels its members are pledging. Each depends on the others, and each is being undermined by military escalation.

Trump told NBC: "We're very close to a deal, or I'm going to blow the hell out of them." Tehran wants sanctions waivers, access to frozen oil revenue, a lifted port blockade, and continued leverage over Hormuz. Neither side has shown the kind of flexibility that produces agreements.

For India, the stakes are not abstract. Every week the strait remains closed costs the economy in higher fuel prices, wider fiscal deficits, and inflationary pressure that reaches from diesel pumps to grocery stores. The monsoon season's early promise has offered some relief on the agricultural side, but the energy equation remains unresolved.

Sunday's Beirut strike was a reminder that the conflict's trajectory is being shaped by actors whose interests do not include India's energy security — but whose decisions determine it.
